[Matthew Butterick makes an excellent point about textbook sizes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W-ryv6TwQvM)

When Matthew Butterick compared "The C Programming Language" to the Applescript book (900 pages by the way!) it confirmed a belief that I had deep within me, and that is that attention is a crucial resource, and focusing it on a small working set of information is exactly the skill we need to be cultivating.

With generative AI, it's so easy to generate a large volume of low quality text. There's so much of it, that it permeates everything that exists online. 

I think it was Paul Graham that discussed how all communication channels eventually turn to 90% entropy. It happened with mail, it happened with phone calls, and it happened with email. Abundance breeds waste. But we _do not,_ and _cannot_ have abundant attention. Each moment of life is precious. Until, of course, the longevity-maxxers unlock 1000 year lifespans and we learn to waste 900 of them.

Here's another great tweet:
![[Pasted image 20261022210405.png]]
https://x.com/bayeslord/status/2108027379562205291?s=20

It almost perfectly captures how I feel about the craft of writing. Perfection is approximated by removing everything that doesn't communicate the message. That's an extremely difficult problem. All you have to do is calculate the number of ways to put words on a page, realize only one of them could be considered perfect, and then it's clear.[^1]

[^1]: For fun, I calculated a very rough upper bound. A piece written in english consisting of as about as many words as this post, assuming 1 million unique English words, is about $$1\,000\,000^{250},$$ that's $$1 \times 10^{1500},$$ or written out, 
$$.$$
